summary: Restored 1938-43 L-4 cab built around a 1921 cupola lookout on Mount Pilchuck, now a hiker shelter in a Washington state park.

facts.design: L-4 14x14 ft groundhouse built around the floor of an earlier D-6/cupola cab
facts.status_note: no longer staffed for fire detection; maintained as a hiker shelter/interpretive site

access.note: reached only by trail; within Mount Pilchuck State Park

visit.trail_note: summit trail from Mount Pilchuck State Park trailhead

facts.agency: Washington State Parks and Recreation Commission

events.note: Osborne Fire Finder mounted on a rock pile at the summit, with spotters sleeping in a nearby tent before any building existed
prefabricated cupola lookout house ordered and shipped up via tramline
lookout completed and staffed, first lookout Everett Huff
L-4 cab built around the old cupola; state parks history gives 1941/1942 and NHLR gives 1943 for this same rebuild -- a three-way date conflict
NHLR gives 1957 as when staffing ended; state parks history says fire-detection use continued until after 1960 and willhiteweb says 'in the 1960s' it was last staffed
Everett Mountaineers-led restoration, ~105 volunteers, ~10,000 hours, with Snohomish County Search and Rescue and an Army Reserve helicopter
registered on National Historic Lookout Register, October 7, 1993

evidence.supports: USFS lookout since 1921, present L4 built 1943, staffed until 1957, transfer to state parks, 1989 Mountaineers reconstruction
evidence.quote: Mount Pilchuck Lookout has been a U.S. Forest Service lookout since 1921. The present wooden L4 14x14' groundhouse was built in 1943 and staffed until 1957.

evidence.supports: 1921 cupola, 1938 L-4 cab, last staffed 1960s, restored 1990s
evidence.quote: First used with a D-6 cupola cabin in 1921, the present L-4 cab, built in 1938, was last staffed in the 1960's.

evidence.supports: Osborne Fire Finder on a rock pile and tent shelter before 1918, 1918 prefab order, cable winch and summit blasting, completion by 1921, new 14x14 lookout 1941/42, use ended after 1960
evidence.quote: Initially, the fire spotting was done with an Osborne Fire Finder mounted on a post in a rock pile at Pilchuck's summit, in use sometime before 1918. ... Before construction of a building at the site, fire spotters stayed in a tent nearby. In 1918, the US Forest Service ordered a prefabricated 12' x 12' building to be assembled on the summit of Mt. Pilchuck. US Forest Service personnel improved the trail to the peak and blasted rock at the summit to make room for the small cabin with a cupola on top. To get the materials to the site, a cable winch was constructed to lift loads of supplies above the highest point the pack string could travel. The lookout was completed by 1921 and staffed each summer. A new 14'x14' lookout was built around the old one in 1941 or 1942. This lookout is still standing on the mountain, although it was no longer used for fire detection after 1960.

The fire lookout underwent a major restoration under an agreement between the WSPRC and a non-profit recreation organization, the Everett Mountaineers, in 1989. 105 people volunteered 10,000 hours, with assistance from Snohomish County Search and Rescue and an Army Reserve helicopter.

evidence.supports: 1918 order detail, tramline construction, four tons of material, Everett Huff as first lookout, 1938 L-4 built around cupola floor, 1988-89 restoration, ongoing upkeep
evidence.quote: In 1918, we learn from newspapers that the District Forester ordered a cupola lookout house from Millmade Construction Company of Portland. ... The material for a lookout house weighed nearly four tons including the glass and hardware. ... From 1919 through 1921, the summit had 12 feet blasted to make room for the cupola. A tramline was also built to haul up supplies for the last several hundred feet.
In 1938, an L-4 cab was built around the cupola, retaining the original floor.

evidence.supports: last staffed in 1960s, restoration, continued maintenance
evidence.quote: In the 1960s, the lookout was last staffed.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Three different years given for the L-4 rebuild around the old cupola: 1938 (firelookout.com, willhiteweb), 1941/1942 (Washington State Parks), 1943 (NHLR). Story presents all three rather than picking one.
NHLR says staffing ended in 1957; Washington State Parks says fire-detection use continued until after 1960; willhiteweb says 'in the 1960s.' Story reports both without resolving.

notes_for_editor: Current brief says 'built 1938' as a single fact; sources genuinely disagree across three dates (1938/1941-42/1943) for the L-4 rebuild, and on the exact last-staffed year (1957 vs after 1960). Treat as an open question rather than a correction to one specific year. Fact-check 2026-10-04: corrected footnote attribution on the opening Osborne Fire Finder/tent sentence and the 1918 order/tramline/four-tons sentence, which the story had sourced to NHLR (cite 1); NHLR's entry is a short paragraph that starts at 1921 and says nothing about pre-1918 history, the Osborne Fire Finder, the tramline, or the four tons of material -- that content comes from Washington State Parks (cite 3) and willhiteweb.com (cite 2), confirmed by re-fetching both pages. Also added cite 2 (willhiteweb) to the sentence listing sources for the 1938 L-4 rebuild date, since willhiteweb is the 'detailed trip-report site' the sentence itself refers to and it explicitly states 1938.
